title: A result nobody acted on
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on a general medical ward. At the start of your shift, you see that a potassium result you requested at 16:00 yesterday came back at 20:00 at 6.7 mmol/L. You had left at 17:00 without handing it over, and no one has acted on it.

The patient, Mr Gold, 79, is on spironolactone and ramipril. The nurse says he seems well.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Repeat the potassium, and only treat if it's still high.
options.brief: Delays treatment of a potentially dangerous result.
options.detailed: Repeating the test is reasonable, but an ECG and assessment are needed now, and treatment may be needed before the repeat result is back.

options.text: Assess Mr Gold now, including an ECG and a repeat potassium.
options.brief: A high potassium can cause dangerous heart rhythms.
options.detailed: Even if he seems well, a potassium of 6.7 needs urgent assessment and treatment. An ECG and repeat potassium guide what needs doing.

options.text: Stop his spironolactone and ramipril, and review tomorrow.
options.brief: Part of management, but doesn't address the immediate risk.
options.detailed: Stopping these drugs is likely to be part of his treatment, but on its own it doesn't address a dangerously high potassium now.

options.text: Report the missed result through the incident system before doing anything else.
options.brief: Reporting matters, but his treatment and being open come first.
options.detailed: This should be reported, and you should do it today, but not before assessing and treating him.

options.brief: Your senior needs to know about a missed result and a sick patient.
options.detailed: Your registrar should know so they can support his treatment and any follow-up, and help you reflect on how it happened.

options.text: Explain to Mr Gold what happened, and apologise.
options.brief: Being open with him is part of putting it right.
options.detailed: He has a right to know when something has gone wrong in his care. An honest explanation and apology, once he is safe, is part of your professional duty of candour.

options.text: Ask the night doctor why they didn't act on the result.
options.detailed: The result wasn't handed over, so the night doctor can't be blamed for missing it.

options.text: Assume the result was haemolysed, as he seems well.
options.detailed: Haemolysis can falsely raise potassium, but you can't assume it, especially in a patient on drugs that raise potassium.

explanation.issue: This tests how you respond when a gap in your handover has left an abnormal result unacted on: treating the patient, telling your senior, and being open with him.
explanation.keyDetails: The potassium is dangerously high. He is on drugs that raise potassium. You didn't hand it over. He seems well.
explanation.reasoning: [B] deals with the immediate risk, [E] tells your senior, and [F] is open with Mr Gold. The distractors delay treatment ([A], [C], [H]), deprioritise the immediate actions ([D]), or wrongly blame a colleague ([G]).
explanation.competing: [D] is the hard distractor: reporting is important and should be done today, but the three keyed actions come first.

references.title: Openness and honesty when things go wrong: the professional duty of candour
references.publisher: General Medical Council and Nursing and Midwifery Council
references.note: Being open with patients when something has gone wrong.
